SHOULD THE GOVERNMENT KEEP SUBSIDISING ELECTRIC SCOOTERS?

For nearly a decade, Taiwan's government has offered cash subsidies to residents who trade a petrol scooter for an electric one, part of a broader push to cut urban air pollution. The program has clearly changed the streets: electric scooters, once a rare sight, now make up a significant share of new scooter sales each year.

Supporters argue the subsidy has been a clear success. Electric scooters produce no tailpipe emissions, and studies link the program to measurable improvements in air quality in dense urban areas where scooters are common. Manufacturers also credit the subsidy with helping Taiwan's battery-swap infrastructure expand faster than it otherwise would have.

Critics, however, question whether taxpayer money should keep funding what has become a mature, self-sustaining market. Electric scooters are now competitively priced even without subsidies, they argue, meaning continued payments mostly benefit buyers who would have switched anyway. Some economists suggest redirecting the funds toward public transportation instead, since buses and trains reduce congestion in ways that individual scooters, electric or not, cannot.

There is also a fairness concern. Rural residents, who often rely on scooters for longer daily commutes but have fewer battery-swap stations nearby, benefit less from the subsidy than urban residents do.

As the program comes up for renewal this year, lawmakers face a genuine question: has the subsidy done its job, or does the market still need support to keep improving?

Rural residents receive far more subsidy money than urban residents currently do
Public transportation has already replaced scooters as the main way Taiwanese commuters travel

DO MODERN ZOOS STILL SERVE A PURPOSE?

Zoos have existed in some form for centuries, but the argument for keeping them has shifted dramatically. Early zoos existed mainly for entertainment, displaying exotic animals in small cages for curious visitors. Today, most major zoos describe their mission differently, emphasising conservation, education, and scientific research over simple spectacle.

Supporters point to real conservation successes. Several species that were once nearly extinct in the wild, including certain condors and specific breeds of horses, have been brought back through breeding programs run largely by zoos and connected research institutions. Zoos also fund field conservation work in the animals' natural habitats, using ticket revenue that would not otherwise exist.

Critics remain unconvinced that this justifies keeping animals in captivity. They argue that most zoo animals will never be released into the wild, meaning conservation breeding programs benefit only a small fraction of captive species. Animal welfare researchers have also documented signs of psychological distress in some zoo animals, particularly large mammals that would naturally travel long distances in the wild but are confined to comparatively small enclosures.

Some zoos have responded by redesigning enclosures to better match natural habitats and by ending exhibits for species known to suffer most in captivity, such as orcas and elephants in poorly suited climates. Whether these changes go far enough remains a matter of ongoing disagreement among scientists, zoo directors, and animal rights advocates.

SURVEY FINDS TEENS READING LESS FOR PLEASURE, BUT NOT LESS OVERALL

A new survey of Taiwanese high school students has found that the amount of time teens spend reading purely for enjoyment has fallen by nearly a third over the past five years. Researchers who conducted the survey, however, caution against a simple explanation of "teens don't read anymore."

The survey measured several categories of reading separately: assigned schoolwork, news articles, social media captions and posts, and books read voluntarily for pleasure. While voluntary book reading declined, total reading time across all categories actually increased slightly, driven largely by time spent reading on phones.

Researchers say the shift reflects changing formats rather than a simple decline in literacy engagement. "Students are reading constantly, just not always in the form parents recognise as reading," said Professor Chen Hui-ling, who led the study. She noted that many students read serialised web novels and fan fiction, categories the survey initially struggled to classify.

Still, some findings concerned educators. Students who read novels regularly scored noticeably higher on reading comprehension tests than students whose reading consisted mainly of short social media posts, suggesting that format may matter for certain reading skills even if overall reading time has not dropped.

The survey's authors recommend that schools introduce more diverse reading formats, including web novels and graphic novels, rather than treating traditional books as the only valid form of reading.

options: Teen reading habits have shifted in format, and this shift may affect certain reading skills
Taiwanese teenagers have almost completely stopped reading anything at all
Total reading time among Taiwanese teens has sharply declined over five years
Schools have already replaced all books with web novels and graphic novels
explain_zh: 文章說明青少年閱讀形式改變（紙本書減少、手機閱讀增加），且格式可能影響閱讀理解能力，最後建議學校引入多元閱讀形式，A 最能涵蓋全文重點。B、C 與文章「total reading time actually increased slightly」相反；D 只是建議，尚未發生。主旨題要注意「形式改變」而非「閱讀減少」才是重點。

Historically, developing a new vaccine took an average of ten to fifteen years, moving slowly through laboratory research, animal testing, and three separate phases of human trials before regulators would approve it for public use. When a new virus caused a global health emergency, this timeline was widely seen as too slow to prevent the disease from spreading further.

Recent vaccine development for that emergency, however, was completed and approved within roughly a year, a pace that surprised even experienced researchers. Several factors made this possible without skipping essential safety checks. First, scientists were able to build on decades of earlier research into similar viruses, meaning they did not start from zero. Second, instead of running trial phases one after another, researchers ran several phases at the same time, with government regulators reviewing data as it became available rather than waiting for a final report.

Funding also played a major role. Governments and private companies invested enormous sums upfront, allowing manufacturers to begin producing vaccine doses before trials had even finished, accepting the financial risk that some doses might later be discarded if trials failed.

Public health experts caution that this speed should not be treated as the new normal for every vaccine. The scale of funding and global cooperation required was extraordinary and difficult to repeat for diseases that attract less public attention or funding.

THE BLACK-FACED SPOONBILL'S REMARKABLE COMEBACK

Every autumn, thousands of black-faced spoonbills arrive at wetlands along Taiwan's southwestern coast, having flown thousands of kilometres from breeding grounds near the Korean peninsula. Recognisable by their distinctive flat, spoon-shaped bills, these birds spend the winter feeding in shallow coastal waters before making the long return journey north each spring.

In the early 1990s, the global population of black-faced spoonbills had fallen to fewer than three hundred birds, placing the species firmly among the world's most endangered waterbirds. Habitat destruction, particularly the loss of coastal wetlands to industrial development, was identified as the primary cause of the decline.

Conservationists responded with an international effort spanning several countries along the birds' migration route. In Taiwan, a major wetland near Tainan was designated a protected reserve after local conservation groups successfully campaigned against a planned industrial project on the site. Similar protections followed in other countries where the birds stop during migration or breed in summer.

Annual population counts, coordinated by researchers across multiple countries, now record more than six thousand birds, a twentyfold increase from the population low. Researchers credit the recovery to coordinated habitat protection rather than any single country's efforts alone, since the birds depend on a chain of safe wetlands stretching across their entire migration route.

Despite this progress, experts warn that continued coastal development in the region means the species' recovery remains fragile rather than fully secured.

A disease that spread quickly among wild bird populations
Competition with other bird species for limited food sources

Dear Wei-Chen,

I hope this letter finds you well. I know it has been a while since I last wrote, but so much has changed since I switched to working remotely last year that I wanted to share my experience, especially since you mentioned considering a similar move at your own company.

At first, working from my apartment felt like a dream. No more crowded commute, no more rushing out the door at seven in the morning. I could start work whenever I wanted, as long as I finished my tasks by the end of the day. For the first few months, I genuinely believed I had found the perfect way to work.

Lately, though, I have noticed some downsides I did not expect. Without colleagues around me, I sometimes go an entire day speaking to almost no one, and I miss the small conversations that used to happen naturally in the office. My manager also seems to expect me to reply to messages almost instantly, since she assumes I am always available now that I am home. The line between "at work" and "off work" has become blurrier than I ever imagined.

I am not saying remote work was a mistake. I still prefer it overall, but I have learned that freedom comes with its own kind of discipline. I now block off specific hours for focused work and make a point of calling a friend or two during the week just to stay connected.

If you do make the switch, my advice is simple: set clear boundaries from the very beginning, before old habits from office life quietly disappear.

Warmly,
Mei-Ling

WHY TEENAGERS NATURALLY WANT TO STAY UP LATE

Parents often blame smartphones entirely when their teenage children resist going to bed early, but sleep researchers say the biology of adolescence itself plays a major role. During puberty, the body's internal clock, which controls when a person naturally feels sleepy, shifts later by roughly two hours compared to childhood.

This shift means that a fifteen-year-old may not feel genuinely tired until around eleven at night, even without any screen use beforehand. The hormone melatonin, which signals to the brain that it is time to sleep, is released later in teenagers than in younger children or adults, making an early bedtime biologically difficult rather than simply a matter of willpower.

The trouble is that school start times rarely adjust to match this shifted clock. Adopting similar changes in Taiwan would require rethinking bus schedules, after-school activities, and parents' own work hours, making reform politically difficult even when the science is clear.

For now, sleep experts recommend that families focus on what they can control: consistent sleep schedules, dim lighting before bed, and reduced screen use in the final hour before sleep.

Five years ago, most small shops and traditional markets in Taiwan dealt almost exclusively in cash. Today, mobile payment apps have become common enough that some newly opened cafés in Taipei no longer accept cash at all, requiring customers to pay entirely through a smartphone app or contactless card.

Central bank data shows mobile and contactless payments now account for a growing share of daily transactions nationwide, with adoption rising fastest among shoppers under thirty-five. In response, several city governments have introduced programs teaching elderly residents how to use mobile payment apps, while consumer protection regulators have signalled they may require businesses to continue accepting cash as a backup option.

For now, cash and mobile payments coexist across most of Taiwan, though the balance between them continues to shift generation by generation.

SHOULD TAIWAN REQUIRE A PERMIT FOR EVERY MOUNTAIN TRAIL?

Taiwan's mountains attract growing numbers of hikers each year, drawn by scenery that ranges from subtropical forest to alpine peaks within a few hours' drive of major cities. This growing popularity, however, has come with a rise in rescue operations, some involving hikers who were poorly prepared for sudden weather changes or trails more difficult than they expected.

Currently, permits are required only for certain high-altitude or ecologically sensitive trails, while thousands of other routes remain freely accessible without any registration. Some rescue workers and park officials argue this system should expand, requiring permits and basic safety briefings for a much wider range of trails, similar to systems used in several other mountainous countries.

Supporters of expanded permits argue that mandatory registration would let rescue teams know exactly where missing hikers likely are, dramatically speeding up search efforts. Briefings could also ensure hikers understand specific trail risks, such as sudden fog or unstable rock sections, before setting out.

Opponents counter that Taiwan's mountains are a public resource that should remain freely accessible, and that permit systems tend to burden responsible hikers while doing little to stop the small minority who ignore warnings regardless of regulation. They also point out that Taiwan's rescue teams are often volunteers whose limited capacity would be strained further by processing permits for thousands of additional trails.

A compromise proposal, still under discussion, would require permits only for trails with the highest historical rescue rates, leaving the vast majority of routes unregulated.

explain_zh: 文章呈現支持與反對擴大登山證制度的論點，並提到折衷方案仍在討論，B 最能涵蓋全文重點。A、D 與文章內容不符；C 文章說救援案件「a rise in rescue operations」，是上升而非下降。主旨題要能同時涵蓋正反雙方的論點。

Linguists estimate that roughly half of the world's approximately seven thousand languages will likely disappear by the end of this century, most without ever being fully documented. In Taiwan, several indigenous languages face a similarly urgent situation, with some spoken fluently by only a handful of elderly speakers.

Language loss typically follows a predictable pattern. Younger generations, often under economic or social pressure to speak a dominant national language for education and employment, gradually use their heritage language less, first at school, then at work, and eventually even at home. Within two or three generations, a language once spoken by thousands can be reduced to a small number of elderly fluent speakers, with children understanding only fragments.

Once a language disappears, linguists argue that more than words are lost. Each language encodes a unique way of categorising the world, including specialised vocabulary for local plants, farming techniques, or traditional navigation methods that may have no exact equivalent in other languages.

Efforts to slow this decline include community language nests, where young children are cared for entirely in the heritage language, and documentation projects that record elderly speakers before their knowledge disappears entirely. Digital tools have also helped; smartphone apps now allow younger community members to learn basic vocabulary and grammar at their own pace.

Success remains uneven. Some communities have seen a genuine revival among younger speakers, while others continue losing fluent speakers faster than new ones can be trained.

explain_zh: 文章說明語言消失的普遍現象與原因，也提到語言巢、記錄計畫、App 等挽救努力，成效不一，C 最能涵蓋全文重點。A、D 過度誇大；B 與文章開頭全球語言消失的敘述不符。主旨題要平衡文章中「消失危機」與「挽救努力」兩個面向。
